claims.text: NbMoTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloys can have high yield strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Achieving a favorable combination of strength and plasticity is difficult in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Carbon can be introduced as an interstitial alloying element in high-entropy alloys.
Adding approximately 0.1–0.5 wt% carbon during vacuum arc melting will promote carbon dissolution in a refractory HEA.
A modest carbon addition will cause in situ formation of finely dispersed carbide precipitates in a refractory HEA.
The carbon-induced carbide precipitates will be nanoscale and coherent with the matrix.
Interstitial carbon increases the local chemical driving force for carbide precipitation.
Fine carbide precipitates inhibit or pin dislocation motion.
Dislocation pinning by the carbides will increase alloy strength.
Coherent carbides locally elevate stress and activate additional deformation mechanisms such as nanotwinning or transformation-induced plasticity.
Transformation-induced plasticity is a known route to exceptional strength and ductility in a metastable dual-phase HEA.
The carbon-induced deformation mechanisms will improve strain hardening.
Improved strain hardening will delay plastic instability and increase ductility.
Relative to a carbon-free refractory HEA, the carbon-alloyed variant will have higher yield strength.
Relative to a carbon-free refractory HEA, the carbon-alloyed variant will have higher uniform elongation.
A low, optimal carbon content will improve the strength–plasticity balance without causing embrittlement.
Carbon contents above an upper limit will produce coarse carbides and embrittlement, eliminating the ductility benefit.
The proposed benefit is expected after vacuum arc melting and homogenization and under room-temperature tensile testing at standard strain rates.
A carbon-free refractory HEA has limited plasticity because it lacks additional strain-hardening mechanisms.
